indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.2.2: Understand mixtures, types, formation, uses and ways of separating them into their components
indicator.objective: Describe a solid-liquid mixture and explain how to separate the components

skills.description: Explain ways to separate a solid-liquid mixture
Give examples of solid-liquid mixtures from everyday life
Demonstrate or describe how to separate a given solid-liquid mixture

misconceptions: Salt and water is not a mixture because the salt disappears.
You can separate sand and water by simply picking the sand out with your hands.
Filtering works for separating salt from water.
Evaporation is the same as boiling.
All mixtures can be separated the same way.

questions.stem: What is a solid-liquid mixture?
options: A solid mixed with another solid
A solid mixed with a liquid
A liquid mixed with a gas
hints: One part is solid, one is wet.
questions.explanation: A solid-liquid mixture is formed when a solid and a liquid are put together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mixture is only when two liquids are mixed.

questions.stem: Which of these is a solid-liquid mixture?
questions.explanation: Sand and water is a solid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse solid-liquid mixtures with liquid-liquid mixtures.

questions.stem: How can you separate sand from water?
hints: Use a filter or a sieve.
questions.explanation: Sand can be separated from water by filtering, which traps the sand while the water passes through.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you can just let it sit (settling/decanting is also valid, but filtering is the standard answer for separating an insoluble solid).

questions.stem: When you mix gari and water, what type of mixture do you get?
questions.explanation: Gari and water form a solid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is a liquid-liquid mixture because it looks wet.

questions.stem: Which of these is a solid-liquid mixture?
hints: It is a solid mixed with a liquid.
questions.explanation: Sugar and water is a solid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is not a mixture because the sugar dissolves.

questions.stem: Ama mixes sand and water. She wants to separate them. What should she use?
questions.explanation: A filter traps the solid sand particles while allowing the liquid water to pass through.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a spoon can separate them completely.

questions.stem: Kwame mixes salt and water. How can he get the salt back?
options: By picking it out with his hands
hints: The water can turn into gas.
questions.explanation: Salt is dissolved in the water, so filtering will not work. The water must be evaporated to leave the salt crystals behind.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think filtering works for dissolved substances.

questions.stem: Which of these describes a solid-liquid mixture?
options: A solid that dissolves or floats in a liquid
Two liquids that do not mix
A gas mixed with a solid
Two solids that are stuck together
hints: One part is solid, one is liquid.
questions.explanation: A solid-liquid mixture contains a solid and a liquid combined, whether the solid dissolves or not.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think mixing only refers to things that don't dissolve.

questions.stem: Give one example of a solid-liquid mixture you can make in the kitchen.
hints: Do you mix a powder with a liquid?
questions.explanation: Salt and water or sugar and water are common solid-liquid mixtures.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a solid-solid mixture like salt and pepper.

questions.stem: What method can you use to separate sand from water?
questions.explanation: Filtering or settling/decanting can be used to separate sand and water.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how you would separate a mixture of sand and water using a filter.

criteria.description: Pours the mixture through the filter
Observes the sand trapped in the filter and the water passing through

hints: Put the filter in a funnel.
questions.explanation: This demonstrates filtering as a separation method for an insoluble solid-liquid mixture.

questions.stem: Why does filtering NOT separate salt from water?
options: Because the salt dissolves and passes through the filter with the water
Because water is thicker than salt
hints: Can you see the salt in the water?
Does it stay on the filter?
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves into tiny particles that pass through the filter along with the water. It does not get trapped.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think filtering separates all mixtures.

questions.stem: Ama has a mixture of sand and water. She leaves it in a cup for a long time. The sand settles at the bottom. What is this process called?
hints: The solid falls to the bottom.
questions.explanation: When a solid settles to the bottom of a liquid over time, it is called settling or sedimentation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the term for this.

questions.stem: Which of these is true about a solid-liquid mixture?
options: The solid and liquid keep their own properties
They always form a new substance
The liquid always turns into a solid
questions.explanation: In a mixture, the original solid and liquid keep their own properties.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mixture creates a new substance.

questions.stem: Write down two solid-liquid mixtures and state one way to separate each.

criteria.description: States a correct separation method for each

hints: Sand and water, salt and water.
questions.explanation: Sand and water can be separated by filtering. Salt and water can be separated by evaporation.

questions.stem: Describe how you would separate a mixture of salt and water in the classroom.

criteria.description: States that the mixture should be heated or left in the sun
States that the water will evaporate, leaving salt crystals behind

questions.explanation: Heating or leaving the mixture in the sun causes the water to evaporate, leaving the solid salt behind.

questions.stem: Explain why you would use a different method to separate salt and water than the method used for sand and water.

criteria.description: States that sand does not dissolve, so it can be filtered out
States that salt dissolves in water, so evaporation is needed to separate it

hints: Can you see the sand in the water?
Can you see the salt in the water?
questions.explanation: Sand is insoluble and can be trapped by a filter. Salt is soluble and passes through the filter, so evaporation is needed to recover it.

questions.stem: A student filters a mixture of salt and sand in water. What is on the filter paper and what is in the water that passes through?
options: Sand on the filter, salt water passes through
Salt on the filter, sand water passes through
Both salt and sand on the filter
hints: Which one passes through the holes?
questions.explanation: The sand is trapped on the filter paper because it does not dissolve. The salt dissolves in the water and passes through the filter.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think filtering separates everything.

questions.stem: A farmer has muddy water and wants clear water. Which two processes can he use?
questions.explanation: Settling allows the mud to fall to the bottom, and filtering removes the remaining fine particles to make the water clearer.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think boiling makes water clear.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what a solid-liquid mixture is and give one example.

criteria.description: States it is a solid mixed with a liquid
Gives a valid example (e.g., sand and water)

hints: Think about a mixture where one part is wet and one part is dry.
questions.explanation: A solid-liquid mixture is a solid combined with a liquid, like sand and water.
